en.title: Compound words
en.summary: A compound word joins two or more words into a new meaning.

paragraphs: A compound word is made of two or more words that together have a single meaning, which is often not the sum of the parts. English forms compounds very freely. They may be written as one word, as two words or with a hyphen, and the spelling has to be learned.

blocks.html:
TypeExamplesStress
noun + nounbedroom, football, traffic light, bus stopfirst part: BEDroom
adjective + nounblackboard, greenhouse, highwayfirst part: BLACKboard
verb + nounwashing machine, swimming poolfirst part
noun + verb-erbus driver, shopkeeperfirst part
verb + prepositiontakeaway, breakdown, check-infirst part
adjective + noun (not a compound)a black BOARD (any board that is black)second part

paragraphs: The plural ending goes on the last word of most compounds: toothbrushes, bus stops. In compounds with a noun first and a preposition, the first noun takes the plural: mothers-in-law, passers-by. A compound adjective with a number is singular: a ten-minute walk.

The first word describes the second: a bus stop is a stop for buses; a stop bus would be a different thing. In English, noun + noun compounds are very common, and the order matters: a house boat and a boat house are not the same.

items: Wrong: **a ten-minutes walk** Right: **a ten-minute walk**
Wrong: **the shop of shoes** Right: **the shoe shop**
Wrong: **a bus's stop** Right: **a bus stop**
Wrong: **a girl friend** (for some uses) Right: **girlfriend**; check a dictionary for each compound.
